objectives.text: Classify carbohydrates as fast- or slow-releasing and give examples of each.
Trace carbohydrate digestion from mouth to colon and say what is absorbed where.
Name the four functions of carbohydrate in the body, including protein sparing.
Distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes in terms of insulin.
Explain what the colonic microbiota do with the carbohydrate we cannot digest.

terms.gloss: A single sugar unit — glucose, fructose, galactose.
Two sugar units joined — sucrose, lactose, maltose.
The storage form of glucose in liver and muscle. Liver glycogen serves the blood; muscle glycogen serves the muscle.
Enough dietary glucose means the body need not break down protein to make it.
A ranking of how quickly a carbohydrate food raises blood glucose.
The bacteria living in the colon. They ferment the fibre our own enzymes cannot digest.

questions.why: Starch is a polysaccharide — long chains that take time to break down. Mono- and disaccharides are the fast-releasing ones.
distractorNotes: A disaccharide, and fast-releasing.
A disaccharide, and fast-releasing.
A monosaccharide, the fastest kind.

questions.prompt: Carbohydrate digestion begins where, and with what?
options: The small bowel, with pancreatic juice
questions.why: Chewing supplies the mechanical half and salivary amylase the chemical half. Both start before the food is swallowed.
distractorNotes: Acid largely halts amylase; protein digestion starts here.
Digestion continues there, but it did not begin there.
Only the indigestible remainder reaches the colon.

questions.prompt: After absorption, monosaccharides are delivered first to:
questions.why: Absorbed sugars travel by the portal vein to the liver, which decides what is stored, converted or released.
distractorNotes: Muscle takes glucose up, but not first.
Storage as fat comes later, and elsewhere.
The pancreas senses glucose; it is not the first destination.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest example of protein sparing?
options: Adequate glucose stops protein becoming glucose
Protein and carbohydrate are absorbed together
Dietary protein slows the absorption of carbohydrate
Extra protein is converted into glycogen
questions.why: Without enough dietary carbohydrate the body makes glucose from amino acids. Adequate carbohydrate spares protein for its own jobs.
distractorNotes: True of a mixed meal, but not what the term means.
A real effect, but a different one.
Protein can yield glucose, but that is the opposite of sparing.

questions.prompt: Liver glycogen differs from muscle glycogen in that:
options: Liver glycogen can restore blood glucose
Muscle glycogen is the larger reserve
Liver glycogen is drawn on only during exercise
Muscle glycogen is released into blood
questions.why: The liver can release glucose into the bloodstream for the whole body. Muscle keeps its glycogen for its own contraction.
distractorNotes: Muscle does hold more in total, but that is not the functional difference.
The liver's reserve is drawn on between meals as well.
Muscle cannot export glucose back to the blood.

questions.prompt: Type 1 diabetes is best described as:
questions.why: Type 1 is insulin deficiency and is treated with injected insulin. Type 2 begins as resistance to insulin that is present.
distractorNotes: That is type 2 — resistance rather than deficiency.
The opposite of the problem.
Insulin structure is not what differs.

questions.prompt: What do colonic bacteria do with fibre that reaches them?
options: Return it to the small bowel
questions.why: Our own enzymes cannot break fibre down, so it arrives in the colon intact and the resident bacteria ferment it.
distractorNotes: Bacteria break it down; they do not absorb it as-is.
Fermentation does not rebuild starch.
Movement through the tract runs one way.

questions.prompt: Why does fibre reach the colon undigested in the first place?
options: We make no enzyme that breaks it down
Fibre passes the small bowel too quickly
Fibre is absorbed and then re-secreted
questions.why: It is an enzyme gap, not a timing problem. That gap is exactly what makes fibre available to the microbiota.
distractorNotes: Transit speed is not the reason.
Fibre is not absorbed at all.
Acid does not create the indigestibility.

questions.prompt: The RDA for carbohydrate in adults is set at 130 g/day mainly to:
options: Prevent the loss of muscle glycogen
questions.why: That figure is the amount needed to supply the brain, which relies heavily on glucose. It is a floor, not a recommended intake.
distractorNotes: Muscle glycogen matters, but is not the basis for this number.
Fibre has its own separate recommendation.
Weight is not what the figure is derived from.

questions.prompt: Which change matches the Dietary Guidelines' advice on carbohydrate?
options: More whole grains, fewer added sugars
Fewer whole grains, more added sugars
questions.why: The direction is toward slow-releasing carbohydrate and fibre, and away from added sugar and refined grain.
distractorNotes: Exactly backwards.
Carbohydrate is not to be eliminated.
Refining is what the advice moves away from.

checklist: Pick one carbohydrate food you ate and classify it fast- or slow-releasing.
Say what happens to it in the mouth, small intestine and colon.
Name which part of it your own enzymes cannot digest.
Say what the colonic bacteria do with that part.
selfCheck: Did I distinguish digestion from absorption?
Did I name an actual enzyme rather than saying 'enzymes'?
applicationPrompts.aiPolicy: These are questions for you to answer. This app does not write any part of a submission.
